source.title: Feedback Gradient Descent: Efficient and Stable Optimization with Orthogonality for DNNs

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper develops and evaluates FGD as an orthogonality-based training method, but does not test the listed claim versions. Its reported training-loss curves do not measure training classification error.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test accuracy and training time for its orthogonality method, but those outcomes do not test the listed versions. Figure 2b shows training-loss curves for WideResNet 28-10 on CIFAR-100; the text describes relative smoothness but gives no exact loss values. Cited findings about other methods are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study develops an optimizer that maintains orthogonality and evaluates its performance. It does not compare initializations, training classification error, spurious minima, shortcut or normalization effects, or learning-rate stability thresholds. Orthogonality during training and distance to the Stiefel manifold do not measure the initialization and loss-curvature effects named by the versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that FGD combines competitive accuracy and computational efficiency with stable maintenance of orthogonality. Numerical stability here primarily means staying close to the Stiefel manifold, rather than stability relative to a loss-curvature learning-rate threshold.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes FGD, an orthogonality-based optimization algorithm; it does not use the original claim's experimental recipe to measure training classification error.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper restricts which convolutional parameters receive orthogonality constraints by model and experiment; it says the restriction used for ResNet and VGG shows the best performance.

fits_no_version.finding: On WideResNet 28-10 trained on CIFAR-100, the authors report that FGD's task training-loss curve is smoother than OCNN's and SRIP's; the plotted losses exclude those methods' orthogonality penalties.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Maintaining orthogonality with FGD produces smoother task training-loss curves than OCNN and SRIP in this setting.

record.problems: The training-loss values in Figure 2b are not numerically reported in the text. The paper does not report training classification error for the claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results omitted. Test-accuracy and training-time results evaluate the proposed orthogonality method but do not measure a behavior named by the listed versions.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training classification error; corrupted or random labels; effects of model size, early stopping, and regularization on training error.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student optimization, spurious local minima, and extra student neurons.
Training-error degradation with depth, prevention by identity shortcuts, and deep plain or normalization-free training recipes.
Effects of activation-matched initialization on propagation, learning speed, and trainable depth; orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization and orthogonal convolution kernels.
Initial linearized stability limits, loss recovery above those limits, divergence, and sharpness dynamics during full-batch training.
Batch normalization's effects on accuracy gain and learning-rate tolerance, and comparable training without normalization using Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: The depth comparisons report test accuracy, not training error. Batch normalization is used without an ablation. Training without normalization or skip connections is discussed as future work. None supplies an additional test of a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, including on corrupted or random labels; model size, early stopping, and regularization effects.
Teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Depth effects on training error, identity shortcuts, and the specified plain-network or normalization comparisons.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, and orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, loss recovery or divergence, and sharpness dynamics.
Batch-normalization effects on training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.
